beginner.headline: Israel's Leaders Argue About Election Results
beginner.brief: Netanyahu's group of parties lost its majority in Israel's election. A majority means more than half the seats in parliament, the group that makes a country's laws. His Likud party accused Arab-led parties of stealing the election. The Arab-led parties rejected this claim and said it was not true. Israel's security service is checking whether these parties received money illegally from Qatar and Turkey. Qatar said the claims about its money were not true. The Arab-led parties won 19 of the 120 seats in parliament. Gadi Eisenkot's group won 48 seats, while Netanyahu's group won 53. Eisenkot said it was too early to know if anything had happened. He accused Netanyahu of trying to make people think the election results were not fair. Eisenkot could form a government with support from the Arab-led parties.

intermediate.headline: Netanyahu faces criticism over election claims
intermediate.brief: Netanyahu's coalition, a group of parties governing together, lost its majority in Israel's election. Final results showed that neither Netanyahu's bloc, or political group, nor the main Jewish opposition won more than half the seats in parliament. The two Arab party lists won a record 19 of parliament's 120 seats following a sharp rise in turnout among Arab voters. Netanyahu's bloc won 53 seats, while the bloc led by his rival Gadi Eisenkot won 48. These figures could give the Arab parties an important role in deciding who forms the next government. Likud, Netanyahu's party, accused the Arab-led parties of stealing the election. The possibility of illegal funding from Qatar and Turkey is being investigated by Israel's home security agency, Shin Bet. Qatar denied the allegations and accused Israeli politicians of spreading false information about the country. Both Arab parties rejected the claim of wrongdoing, and the Joint List said it had no basis. The agency later clarified that its investigation did not accuse an entire community whose members had voted legally. An election official said there was no basis for claims of a pattern of actions breaking rules protecting fair elections. Eisenkot said it was too early to know whether anything had happened and accused Netanyahu of trying to weaken trust in the results. Netanyahu's critics said he was trying to prevent Eisenkot from agreeing to join forces with the Arab parties.

advanced.headline: Israeli Opposition Challenges Netanyahu's Claims of Electoral Interference
advanced.brief: Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot and Arab-led party leaders denounced Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu over claims of foreign interference after his coalition lost its majority. Netanyahu's Likud party accused Arab-led parties of stealing the election, while the Shin Bet security agency was examining whether they had received illegal financial assistance from Qatar and Turkey. Qatar's foreign ministry dismissed the accusations and charged Israeli politicians with conducting a disinformation campaign against Doha. Neither Netanyahu's bloc nor the Jewish opposition secured a parliamentary majority. The Joint List and Ra'am defied expectations by securing a record 19 of the Knesset's 120 seats after a surge in Arab voter participation. With Netanyahu's bloc on 53 seats and Eisenkot's on 48, the Arab parties emerged as potential kingmakers, whose backing could determine who forms a government. Likud alleged that voters had been bribed to choose Arab parties, following a request by the head of the Central Elections Committee for a security inquiry into suspected foreign interference. Both Arab parties rejected the claim, and the Joint List described it as baseless. What Netanyahu's critics see in the dispute is an attempt to delegitimise the Arab parties and make Eisenkot's only current route to power, an agreement with them, politically impossible. Shin Bet clarified that its inquiry did not implicate an entire community whose members had voted legally. The acting director general of the Central Elections Committee said there was no basis for claims of systematic breaches of election integrity. Eisenkot cautioned that it remained too early to establish whether anything had happened and accused Netanyahu of orchestrating a campaign against the legitimacy of the results. Many Arab Israelis had previously boycotted elections, but their participation was now motivated by a desire to oust Netanyahu's governing coalition. The reported options for forming a government were a Netanyahu–Eisenkot unity administration, a Netanyahu coalition involving defectors from Eisenkot's bloc, or an Eisenkot-led administration backed by Arab parties. Although Eisenkot and all but one member of his bloc had previously ruled out governing with Arab parties, speculation persisted that an agreement might still be reached. A Hebrew University snap poll found that, among voters from each party in the opposition bloc, the most popular option was an Eisenkot minority government involving Ra'am, with the Joint List providing backing from outside the government.
